```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
has_terra <- requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)
has_stars <- requireNamespace("stars", quietly = TRUE)
has_lidr <- requireNamespace("lidR", quietly = TRUE)
```

A map has two coordinates, and a third axis can carry a value measured at each place: terrain height, a count per region, a time stamp. ggplot3d reads the usual spatial objects directly. [terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/) and [stars](https://r-spatial.github.io/stars/) rasters become height surfaces, [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) simple features become markers, paths, flat polygons or prisms, and [lidR](https://r-lidar.github.io/lidRbook/) point clouds become data frames of points. All four packages are optional. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

Planar drawing needs planar coordinates. Data in longitude and latitude are reprojected to the coordinate reference system (CRS) given by `coord_3d(crs = )`, which must be a projected one; data that are already projected are drawn in their own units.

## Terrain from a raster

`geom_spatraster_3d()` draws each layer of a raster as a surface through its cell centres, with height and fill taken from the cell values. Large rasters are resampled to a regular sample of about `maxcell` cells first. The elevation raster shipped with terra covers Luxembourg in longitude and latitude, so it is reprojected to the Luxembourg grid (EPSG:2169).

```{r terrain, eval=has_terra && has_sf, fig.alt="Elevation of Luxembourg as a shaded surface, higher in the north."}
elevation <- terra::rast(system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra"))
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster_3d(data = elevation, maxcell = 4000) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL[["green"]], high = "#E8E2C8", na.value = NA) +
  scale_z_continuous(name = "elevation (m)") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_3d(crs = 2169, aspect = c(1, 1.4, 0.35), axes = "z")
```

Missing cells, here outside the border, leave holes. The same raster also works as ordinary data: `fortify()` returns one row per cell with `x`, `y`, `value` and `lyr` columns, so any layer that takes x/y/z data can draw it.

A stars object uses the same height-surface layer. Convert a small part of
the built-in volcano matrix to a stars array; its horizontal positions are
matrix-cell coordinates. Each band becomes a separate surface, with the
computed layer name available for grouping or faceting.

```{r stars-terrain, eval=has_stars, fig.alt="A height surface from a stars array containing sampled volcano elevations."}
terrain_stars <- stars::st_as_stars(volcano[seq(1, 87, by = 3), seq(1, 61, by = 3)])
ggplot() + geom_spatraster_3d(data = terrain_stars, maxcell = 700) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL["green"], high = "#E8E2C8") +
  labs(z = "height (m)") + coord_3d(aspect = c(1.4, 1, 0.7))
```

The regular cell sample controls the amount of geometry drawn. Fortifying
the raster directly returns its full resolution. See
[geom_spatraster_3d()](../reference/geom_spatraster_3d.html) for raster inputs
and the computed values.

## Prism maps

Simple features keep their attributes, so any column can be mapped. `geom_sf_3d()` lays polygons on the floor of the box; mapping `height` raises each one into a prism. The counties of North Carolina, with the number of births in 1974 as height:

```{r prisms, eval=has_sf, fig.alt="North Carolina counties raised in proportion to births, with the tallest prisms around the cities."}
nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf_3d(aes(height = BIR74 / 1000, fill = BIR74), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#C9D9E6", high = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  scale_z_continuous(name = "births (1000s)") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_3d(crs = 32119, aspect = c(4, 1.6, 1), elevation = 40, axes = "z",
           backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 144))
```

Prisms of detailed outlines are many faces; the raster backend draws them in a fraction of the time the vector backend needs (see [Backends](backends.html)). Plain `ggplot2::geom_sf()` layers are drawn the same way inside `coord_3d()`; add the 3D coordinates last so they supply the plot's final coordinate system.

## Cross-sections and fence diagrams

A cross-section is the vertical slice of a surface along a line. `stat_profile_3d()` samples the surface along one or more lines and draws the wall between the surface and a base. The surface is interpolated on the same triangles the surface layer draws, so the top of each wall lies on the drawn surface. With several lines this is a fence diagram, as used for geological sections.

```{r fence, fig.alt="The Maunga Whau volcano as a translucent surface with two vertical walls cutting through it."}
volcano_grid <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(nrow(volcano)) * 10, y = seq_len(ncol(volcano)) * 10)
volcano_grid$z <- as.vector(volcano)
sections <- data.frame(x = c(100, 800, 450, 450), y = c(300, 300, 50, 600),
                       group = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
ggplot(volcano_grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.35) +
  stat_profile_3d(line = sections, base = 90, fill = PAL[["orange"]], colour = "grey20") +
  labs(z = "height (m)") +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(870, 610, 300))
```

The computed `distance` gives the position along each line; with `geom = ggplot2::GeomPath` the stat draws the profile line itself.

## Heights stored in simple features

An XYZ geometry stores height as its third coordinate. Build a three-dimensional
line through one row of the volcano grid, preserving the measured elevation
at each vertex. These are local coordinates in metres. The line and surface
share those coordinates.

```{r xyz-features, eval=has_sf, fig.alt="A red XYZ simple-feature line following a measured cross-section on the volcano surface."}
ridge <- subset(volcano_grid, y == 300)
ridge <- ridge[order(ridge$x), ]
xyz <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_sfc(
  sf::st_linestring(as.matrix(ridge[c("x", "y", "z")]))))
ggplot(volcano_grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_sf_3d(data = xyz, inherit.aes = FALSE,
             colour = PAL["red"], linewidth = 1) +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(870, 610, 300))
```

Points and lines with stored Z coordinates use their own heights. A flat
polygon can receive a mapped height to become a prism. Geographic inputs
need a projected target coordinate reference system, as in the county map.
See [geom_sf_3d()](../reference/geom_sf_3d.html) for geometry and height mappings.

## Flows over a map

`geom_arc_3d()` joins two places by a raised arc, as in flow maps. Each arc rises by `height` times its horizontal length, so long flows arch higher. Without z, arcs start on the floor of the box, where a map lies.

```{r arcs, eval=has_sf, fig.alt="Arcs rising from one county to six others over a flat map of North Carolina."}
nc_m <- sf::st_transform(nc, 32119)
centres <- unname(sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_point_on_surface(sf::st_geometry(nc_m))))
hub <- which(nc$NAME == "Wake")
targets <- match(c("Buncombe", "Mecklenburg", "New Hanover", "Pitt", "Guilford", "Dare"), nc$NAME)
flows <- data.frame(x = centres[hub, 1], y = centres[hub, 2],
                    xend = centres[targets, 1], yend = centres[targets, 2],
                    volume = c(2, 6, 3, 2, 4, 1))
ggplot() +
  geom_sf_3d(data = nc_m, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_arc_3d(aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, linewidth = volume),
              data = flows, colour = PAL[["red"]], height = 0.25) +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.4, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(4, 1.6, 0.8), elevation = 35, axes = character(), panes = "floor")
```

## Point clouds

Airborne laser scanning records millions of points on ground and vegetation. lidR reads them as `LAS` objects; `fortify()` turns one into a data frame with `x`, `y`, `z`, `intensity`, `classification` and the other point attributes. A thinned sample of a mixed conifer stand, coloured by height:

```{r lidar, eval=has_lidr, fig.alt="A point cloud of a forest stand with tall tree crowns over a flat ground."}
set.seed(8)
las <- lidR::readLAS(system.file("extdata", "MixedConifer.laz", package = "lidR"),
                     filter = "-keep_random_fraction 0.1")
points <- fortify(las)
ggplot(points, aes(x, y, z = z, colour = z)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = PAL[["green"]], high = "#E8E2C8") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, z = "height (m)") +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(1, 1, 0.45), axes = "z")
```

For dense clouds, `geom_point_3d(render = "splat")` with the raster backend draws the points as depth-tested spheres (see [Backends](backends.html)).

## The space-time cube

Hägerstrand's space-time cube shows a movement as a path through two dimensions of space and one of time: time runs up the vertical axis, so a stay at one place is a vertical segment and fast travel is a nearly flat one. With a date-time z, the track draws over a floor map and `scale_z_datetime()` labels the axis. The track below is simulated: a trip across North Carolina with stops at three towns.

```{r cube, eval=has_sf, fig.alt="A path rising through time above a map of North Carolina, vertical where the traveller stays in a town."}
towns <- centres[match(c("Buncombe", "Guilford", "Wake", "Pitt"), nc$NAME), ]
start <- as.POSIXct("2026-05-01 06:00", tz = "UTC")
legs <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  s <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 12)
  rbind(data.frame(x = towns[i, 1], y = towns[i, 2], hours = c(0, 8)),
        data.frame(x = towns[i, 1] + s * (towns[i + 1, 1] - towns[i, 1]),
                   y = towns[i, 2] + s * (towns[i + 1, 2] - towns[i, 2]),
                   hours = 8 + 4 * s))
})
track <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(leg, i) transform(leg, hours = hours + 12 * (i - 1)), legs, 1:3))
track$time <- start + track$hours * 3600
ggplot(track, aes(x, y, z = time)) +
  geom_sf_3d(data = nc_m, inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_dropline_3d(data = track[c(TRUE, FALSE), ], colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_path_3d(colour = PAL[["purple"]], linewidth = 1) +
  scale_z_datetime(date_labels = "%a %H:%M") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, z = NULL) +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(4, 1.6, 2), elevation = 20, axes = "z", panes = c("back", "floor"))
```

The track uses the same projected coordinates as the map, `nc_m`. A track recorded in longitude and latitude is projected first with `sf::st_transform()`, so both share one coordinate system.
